scope: Targeted cycling/endurance evidence investigation for a trained amateur with 7–12 total available training hours/week; not an exhaustive systematic review.
provenance: Deduplicated by DOI, PMID, then exact source URL when no identifier exists. Source-level access is the best actually retrieved extraction; every per-topic extraction retains its own access and provenance. Citation aliases preserve all original source IDs. Metadata-only sources do not establish outcomes. Distinct papers from the same cohort remain separate publications, not independent participant samples.

sources.authors: Joyner MJ, Coyle EF
sources.title: Endurance exercise performance: the physiology of champions
sources.population: Champion endurance athletes; synthesis, not a new cohort
sources.key_results: Performance VO2 is VO2max times sustainable fraction; efficiency converts that VO2 into speed or power. Genetic and motivational factors also decide who becomes a champion.
sources.limitations: Review, not a training trial. Does not prescribe amateur hours.

sources.authors: Bassett DR, Howley ET
sources.title: Limiting factors for maximum oxygen uptake and determinants of endurance performance
sources.key_results: VO2max limited primarily by oxygen delivery. Mitochondrial adaptations improve submaximal endurance by raising fat oxidation and lowering lactate at a given VO2. LT speed integrates VO2max, economy and fractional utilization.
sources.limitations: Review. Training evidence for a-vO2 difference cited is older than Montero 2015.

sources.authors: Skattebo O, Martin-Rincon M, Calbet JAL, Hallen J, Holmberg HC
sources.title: A review of central and peripheral limitations to endurance exercise performance on the road to the Milano-Cortina 2026 Olympics
sources.key_results: Systemic O2 delivery is the primary limiter of VO2max in elite athletes. Mitochondrial density and capillarisation support fractional utilization and extraction, which may exceed 95% in some elite skiers. Most fractional-utilization values in the literature are estimates.
sources.limitations: First publication 2026-03-01, before cutoff. Scarce invasive female data. Not a cycling dose trial.

sources.title: The maximal metabolic steady state: redefining the gold standard
sources.key_results: MLSS as commonly measured underestimates the maximal metabolic steady state. CP is the heavy-severe boundary. Exercise at CP is typically sustainable for about 20-30 min.
sources.limitations: Argumentative review. Sustainability range is typical, not a universal constant.

sources.authors: Galan-Rioja MA, Gonzalez-Mohino F, Poole DC, Gonzalez-Rave JM
sources.title: Relative proximity of critical power and metabolic/ventilatory thresholds: systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.key_results: Pooled r=0.73 between CP and thresholds. VT1 underestimated CP by ~30%, MLSS by ~11%, RCP overestimated by ~6%, VT2 by ~21%. CP and VT2 correlation not significant in subgroup.
sources.limitations: Small study set. Inclusion wording required RCTs, which is an odd filter for correlation studies. Offsets are not individual constants.

sources.authors: Burnley M, Jones AM
sources.title: Power-duration relationship: physiology, fatigue, and the limits of human performance
sources.key_results: Only a small power range is sustainable, below CP. Moderate domain fatigue is slow and largely central; heavy domain involves glycogen-related fatigue; severe domain loses metabolic homeostasis and VO2 rises toward max. W-prime is finite work above CP.
sources.limitations: Review. W-prime is model-dependent.

sources.population: 30 male U23 professional cyclists, VO2max 73.8±2.5, CP 5.48±0.38 W/kg
sources.key_results: Fatigued power profile (after 2000 kJ) varied more across the season than the fresh profile. sources.limitations: Observational, one level of rider, not a randomized volume trial. Abstract punctuation was messy; correlations cited are those explicitly recoverable.

sources.authors: Molmen KS, Almquist NW, Skattebo O
sources.title: Effects of exercise training on mitochondrial and capillary growth in human skeletal muscle: a systematic review and meta-regression
sources.population: 5973 participants; 353 mitochondrial and 131 capillary articles. Well-trained mean VO2max 62.2±6.7, few groups, 97% men
sources.duration: search to 2 February 2022; interventions of varying weeks
sources.key_results: Adjusted mitochondrial content +23±5% ET, +27±5% HIT, +27±7% SIT. Per hour SIT ~3.9x ET and HIT ~1.7x ET. Frequency 6>4>2 sessions/week. Well-trained pooled mito estimate +6.6±6.5% (P=0.046). Per-hour endurance-training estimate in that stratum was not statistically distinguished from zero (P=0.933); imprecise, not proof that extra easy hours cannot change mitochondria. Capillaries per fibre similar across modalities and mostly <4 weeks; not clear in well-trained. Load = volume x intensity.
sources.limitations: ET bin is everything below VT2, not Zone 2. Mostly untrained. Not cycling performance. No newer meta-analysis found through 2026-10-02.

sources.title: Physiological adaptations to interval training and the role of exercise intensity

sources.authors: Cove B, Chalmers S, Nelson MJ, Anderson M, Bennett H
sources.title: The effect of training distribution, duration, and volume on VO2max and performance in trained cyclists: a systematic review, multilevel meta-analysis, and multivariate meta-regression
sources.population: Trained cyclists. Abstract: 41 studies, 81 groups, 797 participants. Inclusion was sex-specific Tier 3 study-mean VO2max (men >=59, women >=54.4 mL/kg/min), not every participant >=59.
sources.duration: interventions >4 weeks; database search closed 23 October 2023; 2025 is the journal issue year
sources.key_results: Abstract point estimates only: training improved VO2max (g=0.42) and time-trial performance (g=0.39); no significant between-model difference. Confidence intervals are not copied because abstract and body intervals disagree. Longer duration was positively associated with both outcomes. No detected association of weekly or total volume with either outcome in the subsets that reported volume.
sources.limitations: POL meant LIT or habitual training plus intervals shorter than 5 min above MLSS or at the highest sustainable intensity, not a measured 80/20 or below-LT1 distribution. Intervals longer than 5 min were non-polarized. Counts are internally inconsistent (abstract 41 studies; discussion 44; 23 randomized plus 21 non-randomized). Do not use body confidence intervals. Do not copy the reported weekly volume 4.9 plus or minus 7.3 h (range 2.6-14.3): that SD is implausible for the range. Certainty low. Null volume regression is not a causal optimum or proof that extra hours cannot help.

extractions.authors: Cove B, Chalmers S, Nelson MJ, Anderson M, Bennett H
extractions.title: The effect of training distribution, duration, and volume on VO2max and performance in trained cyclists
extractions.design: Systematic review, multilevel meta-analysis, multivariate meta-regression
extractions.population: Abstract reports 41 studies and 797 participants. Not every cyclist had VO2max >=59. Methods 2.2 (parent PDF handoff, not opened by PHY): Tier 3 group-mean cut, men >=59 and women >=54.4 mL/kg/min. Body 3.2 baseline mean 60.4±4.8, range 54.0-69.1.
extractions.duration: interventions >4 weeks; literature search ended 23 October 2023 (parent PDF); online 2024-12-20, issue May 2025
extractions.key_results: Abstract-reported point estimates: VO2max g=0.42 (0.31-0.53); time trial g=0.39 (0.25-0.53). Longer intervention duration positively associated (VO2max g=0.03, 0.02-0.05; TT g=0.04, 0.03-0.06). No association of weekly or total volume with either outcome in the reporting subset. Authors: beyond a necessary volume, further increases did not appear to enhance performance. That sentence is not a causal optimum. A null polarized vs non-polarized contrast (P>0.05) used their review labels, not a measured 80/20 or below-LT1 split. Cohort mean fitness about 60 mL/kg/min, not a universal individual cutoff of 59. No conflicts declared in the abstract.
extractions.limitations: Study-level association, not a randomized hour dose. PHY retrieved the abstract only and did not independently open the PDF. Parent full-text handoff (2026-10-02): methods 2.2 is a sex-specific group-mean Tier 3 cut (male >=59, female >=54.4 mL/kg/min), so the abstract >=59 wording oversimplifies; body 3.2 baseline is 60.4±4.8 (range 54.0-69.1), not every cyclist >=59. Internal counts disagree and are not treated as validated: abstract 41 studies, discussion 44, body 23 RCT + 21 non-RCT, and 37 acceptable + 7 low also sum to 44. Safe figures used here are abstract 41 studies and 797 participants, g=0.42 and 0.39, and cohort mean about 60. A mean weekly volume of 4.9±7.3 h (range 2.6-14.3) is internally questionable; the 7.3 SD is not used. Search ended 23 October 2023 despite the 2025 issue. DistributionRecovery full-text handoff, also not opened by PHY (section 2.4, p. 424; PDF https://cdck-file-uploads-global.s3.dualstack.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/trainerroad/original/3X/4/c/4c4615506951980ed84df665545b0fc04dd83829.pdf): polarized required a low-intensity or habitual component plus intervals shorter than 5 min at the highest sustainable intensity or above MLSS; longer intervals were non-polarized. That is not 80/20 or time below LT1. Null weekly/total-volume regression used only subsets that reported volume; GRADE certainty for VO2max and time-trial analyses was low. Those limits do not change the published g point estimates and do not show that extra low-intensity hours cannot help.

extractions.title: The effect of training distribution, duration, and volume on VO2max and performance in trained cyclists: A systematic review, multilevel meta-analysis, and multivariate meta-regression
extractions.key_results: Abstract: training improved VO2max (g=0.42) and time-trial performance (g=0.39) with no significant difference between groups labelled polarised and non-polarised. Longer interventions associated with larger VO2max gains; extra volume beyond a necessary amount not clearly additive. This abstract does not establish that the labels were measured 80/20 or pyramidal distributions.
extractions.limitations: Abstract only in this brief (PMID 39788807, first indexed 2024-12-20). Distribution-brief full text, not re-extracted here, classified polarised versus non-polarised by interval duration <5 min, not by measured 80/20 or pyramidal time in zone. Do not use this paper as the polarised-versus-pyramidal comparison. A separate 2025 IPD network meta-analysis using heart-rate time in zones is the better TID contrast and lives in the intensity-distribution brief; this sidecar does not cite its results.

sources.authors: Seiler S
sources.title: What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes?
sources.design: Narrative synthesis of descriptive and intensification studies
sources.key_results: Successful athletes converge near 80% low-intensity sessions and ~20% sessions dominated by high-intensity work. Intensification studies in the already well trained do not convincingly show long-term gains from more HIT emphasis.
sources.limitations: Review/synthesis. Not an interval-format trial. Abstract only.

sources.authors: Seiler S, Haugen O, Kuffel E
sources.title: Autonomic recovery after exercise in trained athletes: intensity and duration effects
sources.population: 9 highly trained male runners (VO2max 72±5, 14±3 h/week) and 8 trained runners (VO2max 60±5, 7±1 h/week)
sources.key_results: In highly trained runners, HRV recovered in 5-10 min after 60 or 120 min below VT1. Threshold and above-VT2 sessions delayed recovery to about 30 min, similarly. Less-trained runners were slower after the same intervals (>=90 min).
sources.limitations: Runners, small n, acute autonomic marker, no 4 h arm, not an adaptation trial.

sources.authors: Mateo-March M, et al.
sources.title: Training characteristics of male and female WorldTour professional road cyclists before the competitive phase
sources.population: 16 female (age 26±5) and 16 male (age 29±6) WorldTour road cyclists
sources.duration: 10 weeks before the first competition of the season; published 23 February 2026
sources.key_results: Sessions 5.9±0.9 vs 6.0±0.9 per week. Hours 16.7±2.6 vs 19.1±2.7 (p=0.016). Week-9 peak 20.1±3.2 h and 22.5±2.8 h; week-10 taper 11.2±4.6 h and 17.7±4.9 h. sources.authors: Sylta Ø et al.
sources.title: The effect of different high-intensity periodization models on endurance adaptations
sources.duration: 12 weeks, 24 interval sessions plus high LIT
sources.key_results: Increasing was 4x16 then 4x8 then 4x4 (mean session lactate about 4.7, 9.2, and 12.7 mmol/L: longer and lower intensity first). Decreasing was the opposite (shorter, higher intensity first). Mixed alternated formats. All improved about 5-10% in 40-min power, peak power, and VO2peak. No 12-week group difference. Neither order isolates a pure threshold-then-VO2 or VO2-then-threshold sequence.
sources.limitations: Candidate for the prompt's sequencing claim; transcript not supplied. Abstract only. Do not map increasing to VO2-first or decreasing to threshold-first.

sources.authors: Odden I, Nymoen L, Urianstad T, Kristoffersen M, Hammarström D, Hansen J, Mølmen KS, Rønnestad BR
sources.title: The higher the fraction of maximal oxygen uptake is during interval training, the greater is the cycling performance gain
sources.design: 9-week training intervention; %VO2max measured every session; regression plus post-hoc median split, not randomized to high vs low fraction
sources.population: 22 well-trained cyclists, 19 men 3 women, VO2max 67.1±6.4 mL/kg/min
sources.duration: 9 weeks, ~21 sessions of 5x8 min at PO40min, three work-rate patterns in randomized order
sources.key_results: Mean interval %VO2max associated with gains in VO2max (R2adj 0.54, p=0.029; multivariate model including baseline, sex, mass change; slope 0.25 mL/kg/min per percentage point), Wmax (R2adj 0.44), power at 4 mmol (R2adj 0.25), and a performance index (R2adj 0.36). No association with 15-min power (p=0.215) or Hb mass (p=0.853). Post-hoc high vs low fraction: VO2max +5.23 vs +1.78 mL/kg/min. High-fraction half did more zone 1 (3:12 vs 1:48 h) and tended to train more total hours (9:43 vs 7:40). Time≥90% only tended to relate to VO2max change. RPE and lactate did not separate the halves.
sources.limitations: Association not causation. Post-hoc split. Easy-volume imbalance. Three women. R2adj is not fraction-alone variance. Title overclaims.

sources.title: Short intervals induce superior training adaptations compared with long intervals in cyclists - an effort-matched approach
sources.design: Randomized 10-week training comparison, effort-matched not power-matched
sources.population: Trained-to-well-trained male competitive cyclists; 20 randomized, 9 short and 7 long completers
sources.key_results: SI: 3x13x30/15, 3 min between series. LI: 4x5 min, 2.5 min recovery. Recovery 50% of work power. Work power 363±32 vs 324±42 W. RPE and lactate similar. VO2max +8.7±5.0% vs +2.6±5.2% (p≤0.05). Wmax +8.5±5.2% vs +1.6±3.6%. Power at 4 mmol +12±9% vs +5±6% (between-group p=0.12). 40-min power +12±10% vs +4±4% (p=0.056). 5-min +8±7% vs +3±7% (ns between groups). 30-s Wingate +5±3% vs +1.4±3.7% (p=0.10). Authors infer time≥90% VO2max as cause but did not measure VO2 during training.
sources.limitations: Male only. Small n. Dropouts. Effort matching confounds duration with power. Mechanism not measured in this trial.

VO2max +8.7±5.0% vs +2.6±5.2% (p≤0.05). Wmax +8.5±5.2% vs +1.6±3.6%. Power at 4 mmol +12±9% vs +5±6% (between-group p=0.12). 40-min power +12±10% vs +4±4% (p=0.056). 5-min +8±7% vs +3±7% (ns between groups). 30-s Wingate +5±3% vs +1.4±3.7% (p=0.10). Authors infer time≥90% VO2max as cause but did not measure VO2 during training.
extractions.limitations: Male only. Small n. Dropouts. Effort matching confounds duration with power. Mechanism not measured in this trial.

sources.limitations: Abstract only. Very short. Elite male-dominated sample. One lab.

sources.title: Time spent at or near VO2max during high-intensity interval training: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of acute tVO2max, search to September 2025
sources.key_results: Long work intervals (≥2 min) elicited more time near VO2max than short (≤30 s) or moderate bouts. Variable-intensity intervals beat even pacing (SMD 0.80). sources.limitations: Acute synthesis. Short category is not specifically 30/15 series. Mixed populations. Opening full text plus abstract; subgroup tables not fully extracted.

sources.authors: Norte BR, Slinn MM, Johnson KO, Mahon E, Shepherd SO, Strauss JA, Louis JB
sources.title: Graded Carbohydrate Ingestion up to 120 g·h−1 Attenuates the Reduction in Critical Power Following 3 h of Moderate-Intensity Exercise in a Dose-Dependent Manner
sources.design: Crossover, 3 h at 95% GET with 0, 60 or 120 g/h CHO, 3-min CP estimate
sources.key_results: After 24 h of 8 g/kg CHO plus a 2 g/kg meal, 3 h at 95% of estimated gas-exchange threshold (GET; first threshold, moderate domain, not FTP). Estimated CP: fresh 277±27 W; water 236±30; 60 g/h 257±28; 120 g/h 266±29. W' fell with no CHO-condition difference. 90 g/h was not tested. Six GI symptoms every 30 min (Figure 7): only 4/16 participants scored ≥4 and <8 in the 60 or 120 g/h conditions. Cumulative scores higher at 120 vs water (p=0.005; 18 [0-81] vs 6 [0-56]) but 120 vs 60 and 60 vs water not significant. Peak regurgitation, fullness and cramps higher at 120 vs water only; no 120-vs-60 difference.
sources.limitations: 3-min estimate of CP; modest VO2max; n=16; 90 g/h not tested. Section heading says GI discomfort was not altered, but post hoc tests show 120 g/h worse than water on cumulative score and three peak symptoms. Not universal tolerance or intolerance. GET preload is not an FTP ride.

sources.title: Systematic review: Carbohydrate supplementation on exercise performance or capacity of varying durations
sources.design: Systematic review of randomised CHO vs placebo performance studies

sources.authors: Wilson PB
sources.title: A narrative review of the high-carbohydrate fueling revolution (≥100 g/h) in the professional peloton
sources.design: Narrative review; open full text read for key points and ACSM quotation
sources.population: Professional cycling context; synthesises laboratory trials
sources.duration: Single-session and multi-day racing discussed separately
sources.key_results: Experiments comparing ≥100 g/h with 60-90 g/h do not clearly show less endogenous carbohydrate use or better performance. Studies do not mimic multi-day stage racing. Possible risks include gut symptoms and, if over-applied in training, a smaller metabolic signal. Quotes 2016 ACSM statement that events ≥2.5 h are associated with better performance up to 90 g/h.
sources.limitations: Narrative review. Multi-day benefit is theoretical/observational, not an RCT.

extractions.limitations: Heterogeneous. Used as review context, not a single effect size.

sources.authors: Tyler CJ et al.
sources.title: The Effects of Heat Adaptation on Physiology, Perception and Exercise Performance in the Heat: A Meta-Analysis
sources.duration: Most often 7-14 days; longer >14 days more effective
sources.key_results: Moderate benefit on exercise capacity and performance in the heat. Longer regimens more effective. Lowers core temperature and supports cardiovascular stability and heat loss.
sources.limitations: Performance synthesis is in the heat, not cool cycling. Large methodological heterogeneity.

sources.authors: McDonald P et al.
sources.title: Influence of Exercise Heat Acclimation Protocol Characteristics on Adaptation Kinetics
sources.key_results: Plasma volume +5.6% (90% CrI 3.8 to 7.0). Time-to-exhaustion +49% (35 to 61). Time-trial +3.1% (1.8 to 4.5). Extra exposure associated with +1.9 g haemoglobin mass (0.6 to 3.2), an across-study slope.
sources.limitations: Heat-performance outcomes. Hb-mass slope is not a daily prescription.

sources.authors: Périard JD, Racinais S, Sawka MN
sources.title: Adaptations and mechanisms of human heat acclimation
sources.key_results: Heat acclimation improves sweating, skin blood flow, lowers body temperature, reduces cardiovascular strain, and can improve hot and potentially temperate aerobic performance. Dose depends on intensity, duration, frequency, and number of exposures.
sources.limitations: Review, not a new trial. Temperate benefit described as potential.

sources.title: Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat

sources.authors: Daanen HAM, Racinais S, Périard JD
sources.title: Heat Acclimation Decay and Re-Induction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.duration: HA ≥5 days; decay ≥7 days in longitudinal studies
sources.key_results: End-exercise HR adaptation lost ~2.3%/decay day; core temperature ~2.6%/day. Re-induction faster than original induction for HR and core temperature.
sources.limitations: Protocols poorly standardised. Not haemoglobin mass.

sources.authors: Scoon GS et al.
sources.title: Effect of post-exercise sauna bathing on the endurance performance of competitive male runners
sources.duration: 3 weeks sauna vs 3 weeks control; 31±5 min at 89.9±2.0°C; 12.7±2.1 sessions
sources.key_results: TTE +32% (90% CL 21-43%), equated to ~1.9% TT. Plasma volume +7.1% (5.6-8.7). Red-cell volume +3.5% (-0.8 to 8.1). Performance correlated with plasma and blood volume, not clearly red-cell volume.
sources.limitations: n=6. TTE. Not 3x45. Not cyclists.

sources.authors: Jenkins EJ et al.
sources.title: Mechanisms of haemoglobin mass expansion following heat stress
sources.key_results: Argues long-term heat acclimation (≥5 weeks) can expand Hb mass ~2-4% via erythropoiesis that diverges from hypoxia pathways (renal oxygen tension, plasma-volume signals, cellular stress). sources.limitations: Review claim that every study showed concurrent VO2max gains is stronger than several original trials retrieved here.

sources.title: Heavy strength training effects on physiological determinants of endurance cyclist performance: a systematic review with meta-analysis
sources.design: Systematic review with meta-analysis of controlled trials
sources.population: 262 endurance cyclists (60 women); mean baseline VO2max 61.25 ml/kg/min
sources.duration: Included interventions 5-25 weeks, 1-3 sessions/week; search to February 2025
sources.key_results: Performance g 0.463 (0.109 to 0.817) is a coherent signed result. Efficiency: small beneficial effect, magnitude about |g| 0.353, p=0.012, low certainty. Prose pairs positive point 0.353 with negative 95% CI (-0.619 to -0.088). Figure 3 displays a negative pooled estimate; caption states negative = beneficial. That positive point plus negative interval is a source reporting inconsistency, not a valid signed pair and not a new estimate. Anaerobic power g 0.560; VO2max, pVO2max, MMSS, and anaerobic capacity not significant. GRADE low. Online 2025-07-09; journal issue 2026, 126(1):193-222.
sources.limitations: Low certainty from risk of bias and imprecision; some non-random allocation; no significant moderators so dose is not optimised. Efficiency text point +0.353 with CI -0.619 to -0.088 conflicts with the negative Figure 3 pool; do not treat that pair as one estimate.
sources.year_note: First published online 2025-07-09; journal issue 2026. Same review, not two studies.

sources.population: 36 trained road cyclists, mixed licence levels, 12 per arm
sources.duration: 12 weeks; strength or core twice weekly plus matched cycling
sources.key_results: Strength superior to core and cycling-only for 5-s, 60-s, 5-min, and 20-min relative power. 20-min adjusted change about 0.22 vs 0.07 and 0.06 W/kg. Core beat cycling-only only at 5 s. Body mass unchanged. Reported VO2max was estimated from 5-min power.
sources.limitations: Not blinded; mixed performance levels; exploratory.

sources.authors: Barranco-Gil D, Hernandez-Belmonte A, Rodriguez-Rielves V, et al.
sources.title: Off- and on-bike resistance training in cyclists: a randomized controlled trial
sources.population: Well-trained male cyclists; off-bike n=12, on-bike n=12, control n=13
sources.duration: 10 weeks; 2 sessions/week at 70% 1RM; cycling volume and intensity matched
sources.key_results: No VO2max effect. Strength rose 2.6-5.8% off-bike and 4.5-7.3% on-bike versus -5.8 to -3.9% in control. Wingate +4.1% and +4.3% versus -4.9%. Quadriceps CSA +2.5% and +2.2% versus -2.3%. Epub 2024-09-03; issue 2025-02-01.
sources.limitations: Abstract-only. Not a time trial. Treat with STR13 as one programme, not two replications. Load was 70% 1RM, not 4-10RM.

sources.title: The effects of resistance training on road cycling performance among highly trained cyclists: a systematic review
sources.design: Systematic review of RCTs to September 2009
sources.population: Highly trained road cyclists, more than 7 h/week or 150 km/week

extractions.key_results: Documents 30 s moving average for TSS/NP versus 25 s EWMA for xPower; CTL/ATL default time constants 42 and 7, claimed to relate to fitness and fatigue; TSB = yesterday CTL minus yesterday ATL; session-RPE = post-session RPE x minutes (citing Foster 2001); decoupling >5% heuristic qualified by heat and dehydration.
extractions.limitations: Implementation doc, not a validation trial.

sources.authors: Friel J
sources.title: Aerobic decoupling and heart rate drift explained
sources.key_results: Defines decoupling as first-half versus second-half power:HR. Publishes <5%, 5-10%, >10% bands and states there is no hard research-based rule for how long coupling should last. Lists heat, dehydration, glycogen, and fatigue as causes of drift.
sources.limitations: Updated 2026-06-03. Bands are coaching practice.

sources.authors: Quittmann OJ; Piehl MA
sources.title: The 3-min all-out test in cycling: a systematic review and meta-analysis on its reliability and validity
sources.population: 20 studies, N=284, mostly small and male, 2006-2025
sources.key_results: EP ICC 0.89-0.99 and WEP ICC 0.76-0.98 if retested within 3 weeks with familiarization. EP overestimated CP (gz=0.408, PI 0.024 to 0.792). WEP underestimated W' (gz=-0.389, PI -0.954 to 0.176). Pooled EP vs CP: r=0.993, SEE 21 W, bias +11.7 W, LoA -37 to +61 W. WEP vs W' r=0.499, SEE 5.4 kJ.
sources.limitations: Full text. Heterogeneous protocols. Prediction intervals wide.

claims.conclusion: Sustainable cycling power is the interaction of VO2max, the fraction that can be held, and efficiency, not an FTP trait.
Short-term VO2max gains are mostly oxygen delivery; extraction is already high in well-trained athletes.
Critical power, MLSS, second thresholds and FTP are related and not interchangeable.
Mitochondrial and capillary gains follow training load, not a unique Zone 2 pathway.
Lower gains at higher baseline fitness and a null study-level volume regression are not a randomized weekly-hour dose-response trial.
Progress volume by recoverable steps; a universal 10% rule is not validated for cyclists.
One long ride and two shorter rides of equal time are not known to be equal training stimuli.

No retrieved direct longitudinal comparison ranks 55-60% versus 65-75% FTP. Whether those bands differ in performance adaptation is uncertain. Fixed percentages of maximum misclassify intensity domains on separate evidence.
Research Zone 1, cycling Zone 2 and popular Zone 2 are different constructs.
Riding easier as weekly hours rise is a recovery-oriented coaching choice, not a proven workload rule.
80/20 describes a common high-volume session pattern; it is not an experimentally identified optimum for every volume, phase, or event.

Polarized training has not been shown superior to pyramidal or other non-polarized distributions for trained cyclists' time-trial performance; a small VO2peak edge and older threshold-heavy contrasts are narrower claims.
Session-goal, time-in-zone, and 3/5/7-zone labels are different measurements and must not be treated as interchangeable prescriptions.

When load is matched, ordering 4-, 8-, and 16-minute mesocycles as longer/lower-intensity first versus shorter/higher-intensity first has not been shown to matter over 12 weeks. Neither Sylta order is a pure VO2-before-threshold or threshold-before-VO2 sequence. Elaborate base-build-peak or reverse sequencing is not a demonstrated requirement.
Short HIT or moderate-intensity blocks can improve well-trained cyclists, but superiority over even spacing is conflicting and not established.
About two hard endurance sessions per week is a workable and commonly studied dose, not an experimentally proven optimum versus one or three.
About 48 hours is a reasonable default gap after severe work based on autonomic recovery summaries, not a performance law; multi-hour easy rides are training, not free recovery.
A universal maintenance minimum and an obligatory mathematical deload cannot be prescribed; pre-event tapers have better evidence than routine 3:1 unload weeks.
Distribution should change with volume, days, phase, and event, but specific zone percentages for amateur cyclists are not fixed by factorial trials.

In one well-trained cyclist cohort, higher mean %VO2max during 5x8 min intervals at PO40min was associated with larger gains in VO2max, Wmax, power at 4 mmol, and a composite index. This is not proof that raising the fraction causes the gain.
Time ≥90% VO2max is a noisy acute marker, not a validated surrogate for subsequent adaptation.

Effort-matched 30/15 series can outperform 4x5 min intervals on several outcomes in trained male cyclists, but this is not a universal short-versus-long rule, and the 2015 trial did not measure the proposed time≥90% mechanism.
Ordering 4x16, 4x8, and 4x4 over 12 weeks does not detectably change outcomes when load is matched.
A unique 4-8 minute sweet spot is not established for well-trained cyclists. It is supported only as an intensity-by-duration interaction in one recreational cohort.

Exact 5x5 and isolated 1-minute VO2 formats still lack a trained-cyclist performance head-to-head. 40/20 has one 4-week randomized comparison against 4x8 that did not separate VO2peak; calling any of these optimal remains coaching practice.
Fixed %FTP, %MAP, or %VO2max anchors are weak. Self-paced maximal effort raises acute time near VO2max, especially for longer intervals.
Within-interval power variation sometimes raises acute time near VO2max and sometimes does not. No retrieved trial shows this changes adaptation.
Near-maximal intervals are not uniquely required for endurance gains in well-trained cyclists. RPE and breathlessness are not measurements of %VO2max.
Maximal aerobic power is test-protocol dependent, so an unnamed %MAP target is not portable across ramp designs.
FTP, CP, MLSS and RCP correlate at group level but are not interchangeable for an individual.

Sustainable power is raised by more than one intensity domain. A threshold-heavy week is a viable stimulus, not a proven best or exclusive system. Cove 2025's null polarised versus non-polarised contrast is not a measured 80/20 or pyramidal comparison.
Named FTP recipes and a uniquely efficient sweet-spot band are coaching practice, not trial-established optima.
Threshold and short time-trial power fall after prior work; absolute 1500/2000/3000 kJ cut-points are not universal.
Fresh FTP or VO2max does not fully identify who retains power after prior work.

Durability can improve. Heavy strength twice weekly for 12 weeks improved 5-min power after 185 min in one controlled cyclist study; that does not prove an effect independent of fresh fitness. The optimal endurance-session type is uncertain. No matched fresh-versus-late interval trial was retrieved.

No controlled evidence shows fatigue-state intervals improve late-race performance more than the same intervals done fresh. A higher recovery cost is a plausible risk, not a matched early-versus-late result.

No trial establishes an optimal long-ride duration or weekly share. A 25-40% share of cycling time is an untested coaching span, not a ceiling. One example that already includes strength inside 7/9/12 h is 120/390, 180/480 and 210/660 cycling minutes (~31%, ~38%, ~32%).

Carbohydrate availability can change the moderate-to-heavy transition and estimated CP, but that is not structural durability. Main 2026 is depletion plus 24 h of ≤1 vs ≥9 g/kg CHO, not a skipped breakfast. Norte 2026 used 3 h at 95% GET, not FTP; 120 g/h beat water for preserving CP and raised some GI scores versus water, while 120 vs 60 g/h was not significant and 90 g/h was not tested. Neither universal tolerance nor a fasted long ride as a durability method is supported.

Carbohydrate versus none during prolonged exercise is strong evidence. The hourly target is moderate evidence. Superiority of 100-120 g/h over 60-90 g/h is plausible but uncertain; high dose is optional, not mandatory. The claim grade is Moderate because the practical conclusion is the hourly/high-dose claim, not the placebo contrast.

Glucose or maltodextrin plus fructose, via SGLT1 and GLUT5, raises exogenous oxidation above a single-source ceiling; 2:1 and about 1:0.8 both work, and ratio differences are smaller than mixed versus glucose alone.

Glucose plus sucrose supplying the same overall 2:1 glucose:fructose as free glucose plus fructose oxidised similarly in Trommelen 2017 (10 trained men, 108 g/h; 0.6 g/min glucose + 1.2 g/min sucrose vs 1.2 glucose + 0.6 fructose). Sucrose alone was not tested in that comparison and is not claimed to match a free mix. Separately, sucrose versus glucose protects liver glycogen during moderate cycling and speeds liver, not muscle, repletion. Table sugar is a cheap legitimate carbohydrate, not a proven sports-drink clone.
Oxidation, absorption, and tolerance are separable. Short gut training can reduce symptoms in some runners but does not reliably unlock 120 g/h as a performance requirement.
In-ride and around-session carbohydrate mainly protects session quality and next-day work; it is not evidence of a separate structural adaptation from extra carbohydrate.

Periodised carbohydrate restriction has not reliably improved endurance performance in trained athletes. Gejl 2021 SMD 0.17 (95% CI -0.15 to 0.49) is an imprecise null, not proof of zero or of universal no benefit. Not fasting quality sessions is a risk-oriented practical choice, not proof of a null. A benefit of train-low remains plausible but uncertain.

When rapid glycogen restoration is the goal, about 1.2 g/kg/h early is the rate at which muscle resynthesis is described as maximised. It is not a minimum after every ride. Sucrose or glucose-fructose favours liver glycogen. Even 10 g/kg over 12 h may not fully restore muscle glycogen. Sollie 2023 is design-only here; the title is not an outcome.
Endurance protein needs are credibly about 1.4-2.1 g/kg/day, with point estimates near 1.6-1.8 on hard days; timing is secondary to the daily total unless carbohydrate is inadequate.
Fluid and sodium replacement must be individualised. Overdrinking, not a missed universal sodium dose, is the dominant cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia.

Low energy availability and REDs can limit health and training, but screening is not diagnosis and there is no universal caloric threshold. The share of recovery limited by intake versus programming is not a known percentage.
Acute sleep loss impairs physical performance, including endurance; total deprivation and late restriction are clearer harms than every partial short night, and afternoon tests are more vulnerable.

Nine hours plus a nap is not a proven requirement. Elite athletes often sleep about 6.5-7 h and report needing about 8.3 h; short sleep is strongly tied to schedule, not a demonstrated extra biological need from training hours.

A few nights of sleep extension can maintain endurance time-trial performance better than normal or restricted sleep in a small cyclist crossover; basketball and tennis extension trials do not establish a cycling adaptation dose.

Daytime naps can improve acute physical performance and perceived fatigue, especially 30 to <60 min with a buffer before testing; 20-30 min naps do not reliably avoid sleep inertia, and cycling time-trial evidence is thin.

Severe sleep loss lowers muscle protein synthesis in young adults, and endurance overreaching can reduce objective sleep efficiency, but this is not evidence that ordinary short nights block VO2max or FTP adaptation.

Heat acclimation improves performance and tolerance in the heat more consistently than in cool conditions. Post-exercise sauna or hot-water immersion has uncertain performance effects in meta-analysis.

Plasma-volume expansion within days is not the same as a rise in haemoglobin mass over weeks. A lower haemoglobin concentration after heat or training is often dilution. Heat-driven erythropoiesis is not established as the same mechanism as hypoxia.

Validated heat doses must be stated exactly, and sauna is not hot-water immersion. No retrieved trial specifically tested 3x45 min/week sauna, so that dose should not be declared effective or ineffective. Jenkins 2025 tested 45 min hot-water immersion at 5 sessions/week, a different modality and frequency. Daily sauna has not been shown head-to-head to beat three sauna sessions for the same outcome.

Heat acclimation reduces heat strain but remains a stressor. Dehydration is not an effective haemoglobin-mass strategy. A studied hot-water block did not worsen sleep as an overreaching marker. Maximal heat is not a default amateur prescription, and adaptations decay within days to two weeks.

No indiscriminate supplementation in an iron-replete athlete. Treat documented deficiency under professional assessment, not a ferritin-alone rule. Acute-phase ferritin can mask deficiency; the clinician uses haemoglobin, ferritin, transferrin saturation or other iron markers, inflammation, and context. A normal or high ferritin alone does not exclude deficiency or make treatment categorically contraindicated. Cycling causes less foot-strike haemolysis than running, and one temperate bout loses little sweat iron, but hepcidin versus sweat versus menstrual loss is sex- and context-dependent, not a universal ranking.
Heavy lower-body strength can improve cycling time-trial or time-to-exhaustion performance without a reliable VO2max increase.
Economy and anaerobic power are the more consistent companions of that performance effect; threshold and VO2max are not guaranteed.
Sprint and plyometric work are task-specific and are not a proven replacement for heavy strength.

Low-load core and activation routines are not a required performance method. There is no adequate evidence that they correct a claimed imbalance or prevent cycling injury; that gap is not proof that every such routine is ineffective.
Concurrent interference is real for explosive strength and next-day peak power, but a 6-hour cyclist rule is not established.

Two weekly sessions can build the strength effect and one session often maintains it. Those minutes and their recovery cost count inside a 7/9/12 h total budget by replacing easy cycling (examples 390+30, 480+60, 660+60 min), or add about 1-1.5 h if the hours were cycling-only. This is a supported implementation, not a 30-minute optimum.
A short cycling warm-up changes output; prolonged static stretching can impair isolated force; band activation is not required.
Strength, mobility, and activation have not been shown in adequate cyclist trials to prevent cycling injury or correct imbalances.

TSS, NP, IF, CTL, ATL, and TSB are deterministic bookkeeping models. One hour at the entered FTP is 100 TSS by construction. CTL is not measured fitness. Default 42- and 7-day constants are vendor conventions, not fitted biological time constants.

Equal TSS is not equal physiological stress. Steady-state TSS scales with IF squared, so the same TSS can represent very different kilojoules. A high FTP setting systematically understates TSS and inflates prescribed zones.

Hours, kilojoules, heart-rate TRIMP, and session-RPE answer different questions. They correlate, especially when duration is shared, but are not interchangeable and should not be converted by a universal equation.

TSS and related impulses show dose-response associations with fitness changes in some observational blocks. That does not validate CTL targets, ramp-rate rules, or the default 42/7 constants as decision thresholds.
Acute:chronic workload ratios are not established causal injury models. TSB is a description of recent versus chronic load timing, not a measurement of readiness or injury risk.
Whether a program is working is judged from standardized performance beyond test noise, not from a rising CTL. A 20-minute FTP test can miss a real maximal-lactate-steady-state change.

A 20-minute test is reliable for tracking threshold-domain performance. Ninety-five percent of that power, critical power, and 3-minute end-test power are related but not interchangeable, and none measures VO2max. W' and 3-minute work above end-test power are too noisy or biased for week-to-week decisions.

Heart rate at fixed power, decoupling, resting heart rate, and HRV can show multi-week trends but are too noisy and confounded for single-day pass/fail decisions. The 5% decoupling rule is coaching practice, not a trial endpoint.

Subjective wellness is often more sensitive to acute load than common objective markers. HRV-guided training has small, often non-significant group effects on performance. A composite of HRV, resting heart rate, and wellness is more defensible than HRV alone and is not proven superior to a well-built fixed plan.
When metrics conflict, the repeated performance test and the internal response outrank the smoothed external-load score. The exact weekly checklist is a practical synthesis, not a tested package.
